topic.title: Combined transformations and reflections in y = x and y = −x
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: One or two questions a series across M7 and M8, on either paper, usually among the last five. The 4-mark drawing (reflect in y = ±x, then enlarge by a fractional scale factor about a given centre) appeared as Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q15 and M8 Paper 2 Q8 (just over 40% correct, over 30% with no understanding) and Summer 2024 M7 Paper 2 Q15 and M8 Paper 2 Q6 (nearly half full marks). The 2- or 3-mark "describe fully the single transformation" appeared as Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q12 (rotation), November 2024 M7 Paper 2 Q15 and Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q9 (enlargement, only a minority giving both centre and scale factor) and Summer 2026 M7 Paper 2 Q6. Single reflections in y = ±x carry 2 marks (November 2025 M7 Paper 1 Q16; Summer 2026 M7 Paper 2 Q14 and M8 Paper 2 Q5).
mustMemorise: Reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (a, b) → (b, a)
Reflection in y = −x swaps them and changes both signs: (a, b) → (−b, −a)
Each transformation in a combination acts on the image the one before it made, so the order in the sentence is the order on the page
The first image is worth marks on its own — draw it, label it, leave it
Two reflections in perpendicular mirrors = a rotation of 180° about their crossing point
Two reflections in parallel mirrors = a translation of twice the distance between them
Full descriptions: reflection + mirror line equation; rotation + angle + direction + centre; translation + column vector; enlargement + scale factor + centre
Centre of rotation: perpendicular bisectors of two vertex joins; centre of enlargement: corresponding vertices joined and extended
notOnThisSpec: Rotations through angles other than ±90° and 180° (Teacher Guidance for M6-GM-05)
Negative scale factors, which belong to M8-GM-04

mustKnow: Reflection in y = x: (a, b) → (b, a), the coordinates swap and the signs are untouched
Reflection in y = −x: (a, b) → (−b, −a), swap and then change both signs
Apply the transformations in the order the question states, each one acting on the image the one before it made
Two reflections in perpendicular mirrors = a rotation of 180° about the point where they cross
Two reflections in parallel mirrors = a translation of twice the gap, perpendicular to them
Describe fully: reflection + the equation of the mirror; rotation + angle + direction + centre; translation + column vector; enlargement + scale factor + centre
Centre of rotation: the crossing point of the perpendicular bisectors of two vertex joins
Centre of enlargement: the crossing point of the joins of corresponding vertices, extended

sheet.howExamined: M7 and M8, Paper 1 (no calculator) and Paper 2 (calculator), 50 marks in 75 minutes each; nothing here needs a calculator on either. One or two questions a series, usually among the last five, in two shapes. The drawing shape is 4 marks, marked as first image then final image, two marks each: Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q15 and M8 Paper 2 Q8 both asked for a reflection in y = x and then an enlargement of scale factor ½ about an off-origin centre, and Summer 2024 M7 Paper 2 Q15 asked for the same with scale factor ½ about (7, 2). The describing shape is 2 or 3 marks with one mark per item on the checklist: Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q12 (rotation, 3), November 2024 M7 Paper 2 Q15 and Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q9 (enlargement, 3), Summer 2026 M7 Paper 2 Q6 (2). Single reflections in y = ±x are worth 2 on their own (November 2025 M7 Paper 1 Q16; Summer 2026 M7 Paper 2 Q14 and M8 Paper 2 Q5). Follow-through is normal: a wrong first image that is then transformed correctly still earns the second stage.
traps: Reflecting in an axis, or in y = −x, when y = x was asked for — the single most-reported slip on this topic (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q15, November 2025 M7 Paper 1 Q16)
Doing the swap for y = −x but not changing both signs, or changing the signs without swapping
Erasing the first image once the second stage is drawn, which throws away two of the four marks (Summer 2024 M7 Paper 2 Q15)
Halving or doubling the coordinates instead of the distances from the centre, or drawing the image on top of the centre (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q15)
Describing a single transformation as two joined by "then", which scores zero however accurate it is (Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q12)
Writing "turn" where the scheme wants "rotation", or giving a rotation with no direction or no centre (Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q12)
Naming an enlargement without both the scale factor and the centre — only a minority gave both (Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q9)
Inverting a fractional scale factor, so a shrinking enlargement is called scale factor 3 instead of ⅓ (November 2024 M7 Paper 2 Q15)
Taking two reflections in parallel mirrors as a translation of the gap rather than twice the gap
Applying the second transformation to the original shape instead of to the first image

Reflecting in some other line and then enlarging that image perfectly: the enlargement still earns its own marks, but every coordinate of the final shape is wrong, so draw y = x on the grid before anything moves (Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q8)

Making no start at all because the first stage is a reflection in y = x — nearly half the entry took full marks on this one, and that first stage is only the swapping of each pair of coordinates (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q6)

noteBlocks.lede: Reflecting in $y = x$ swaps a point's two coordinates: $(3, 5)$ becomes $(5, 3)$. Reflecting in $y = -x$ swaps them and changes both signs. Those two sloping mirrors are the only new thing in this topic, and almost every mark that goes missing on the grid question goes missing there.
can: Reflect a point or a shape in $y = x$ and in $y = -x$.
Carry out two transformations in the order given, keeping the middle image.
Describe a single transformation with every detail the scheme wants.

noteBlocks.text: Combined transformations, and the mirrors y = x and y = -x

noteBlocks.md: The line $y = x$ is made of every point whose two coordinates are equal, so it runs at $45°$ through the origin. Reflecting across it exchanges how far along you are with how far up, which is why the coordinates swap. The mirror $y = -x$ swaps them and turns both signs over. Work vertex by vertex and keep every image you draw.

noteBlocks.caption: One point, two diagonal mirrors: (3, 5) becomes (5, 3) in y = x, and (-5, -3) in y = -x.

noteBlocks.prompt: The point $(3, 5)$ is reflected in the line $y = x$. Its image is
noteBlocks.explain: Reflecting in $y = x$ swaps the two coordinates, so $(3, 5)$ becomes $(5, 3)$. That is the whole rule, and the rest of this lesson is about trusting it.

noteBlocks.text: Why y = x swaps the coordinates

noteBlocks.md:
The line $y = x$ is made of every point whose two coordinates are equal: $(1, 1)$, $(4, 4)$, $(-3, -3)$. Reflecting in it is the move that **exchanges the roles of across and up**. Go 3 across and 5 up, reflect, and you go 5 across and 3 up. So $(a, b) \to (b, a)$.

The line $y = -x$ is the other diagonal, through $(1, -1)$ and $(-4, 4)$. It swaps the roles too, but it also turns each direction into its opposite, so $(a, b) \to (-b, -a)$: **swap, then change both signs.**

noteBlocks.prompt: The point $(3, 5)$ is reflected in the line $y = -x$. Its image is
noteBlocks.explain: Swap to get $(5, 3)$, then change both signs to get $(-5, -3)$. Doing only the swap gives $(5, 3)$, which is the $y = x$ answer; doing only the signs gives $(-3, -5)$, which is a half turn about the origin.

noteBlocks.md: **Do it vertex by vertex.** Reflect one corner, mark it, reflect the next, mark it, then join them up. A triangle takes three swaps. The shape below has corners at $(4, 1)$, $(7, 1)$ and $(7, 3)$, so its image has corners at $(1, 4)$, $(1, 7)$ and $(3, 7)$ — and you can read that straight off the list without measuring anything.

noteBlocks.alt: A coordinate grid from -8 to 8. The dashed mirror line y = x is drawn. Triangle A has vertices at (4, 1), (7, 1) and (7, 3), below the mirror line. Its image, triangle A dash, has vertices at (1, 4), (1, 7) and (3, 7), above the mirror line. A dashed segment joins each vertex to its image.

noteBlocks.title: Draw the mirror first
noteBlocks.md: Both diagonals are already a feature of the grid, so drawing them costs about four seconds: $y = x$ runs corner to corner through the origin with a slope of 1, and $y = -x$ is the other diagonal. Every November and every summer the reports record the same slip — the shape reflected in the $y$-axis, or in $y = -x$ when $y = x$ was asked for. A drawn mirror line makes that slip visible to you before it becomes visible to a marker.

options: $y = x$
the $y$-axis
noteBlocks.explain: Each point has a $y$-coordinate that is the negative of its $x$-coordinate, so the line is $y = -x$: the diagonal that falls from left to right.

noteBlocks.title: A ten-second check
noteBlocks.md: After a reflection in $y = x$, every image coordinate should be a swapped copy of an object coordinate: $(4, 1)$ goes to $(1, 4)$, and the two lists should match up pair for pair. After a reflection in $y = -x$, the same check with both signs changed. After an enlargement, count the distances: each image vertex should be $k$ times as far from the centre as its object vertex, measured across and up separately. Three checks, ten seconds, and they catch almost every slip this topic produces.

noteBlocks.title: Reflections - Corbettmaths
noteBlocks.why: Corbettmaths video 272 does the vertex-by-vertex reflection, including the sloping mirrors, at the pace of someone drawing it on a grid. Watch it once, then come back and answer the gate below without pausing it again.

noteBlocks.prompt: Reflect $(-6, 2)$ in the line $y = x$. The image is
noteBlocks.explain: Swap: $(-6, 2) \to (2, -6)$. If you also changed the signs you have reflected in $y = -x$ instead, which is the most common of all the slips on this topic.

noteBlocks.text: Two transformations, in the order given

noteBlocks.md:
A combined question reads like this: *reflect in $y = x$, then enlarge by scale factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ about $(-5, -2)$.* Three rules carry it:

**1 Do them in the order written.** The first transformation acts on the original shape; the second acts on the image the first one made, never on the original.

**2 Leave the middle image on the grid.** It is worth marks on its own. Rubbing it out after using it throws those marks away, and the reports say plainly that candidates do this.

**3 Label as you go.** Call them A, A' and A" so the marker can see which is which.

noteBlocks.prompt: A question says: reflect in $y = -x$, followed by a translation. Which shape does the translation act on?
options: The image made by the reflection
The original shape
Either, because the order does not matter
noteBlocks.answer: The image made by the reflection
noteBlocks.explain: Each transformation acts on whatever the one before it produced. That is why the middle image has to be drawn before you can start the second step.

noteBlocks.md: **The enlargement step, in one sentence:** draw a ray from the centre to a vertex, then put the image of that vertex at $\tfrac{1}{2}$ of the way along it. Vertex $(1, 4)$ is 6 across and 6 up from $(-5, -2)$; half of that is 3 across and 3 up, which lands on $(-2, 1)$. Do the same for the other two. Nothing here needs a ruler measurement — the counting on the grid is exact.

noteBlocks.prompt: Enlarge $(3, 8)$ by scale factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ with centre $(-5, -2)$. The image is
noteBlocks.explain: From $(-5, -2)$ to $(3, 8)$ is 8 across and 10 up. Half of that is 4 across and 5 up, which reaches $(-1, 3)$. Halving the coordinates themselves would give $(1.5, 4)$ and that ignores the centre completely.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2025, M7 Paper 2 Q15
noteBlocks.md: This exact shape of question — reflect in $y = x$, then enlarge by $\tfrac{1}{2}$ about a centre that was not the origin. Reflections in the axes, and in $y = -x$, were common. The scale factor itself was understood; the centre was not, and some candidates drew their image sitting on top of the centre. The same combination was on M8 Paper 2 Q8 that summer, where just over 40 per cent were correct.

noteBlocks.prompt: In a 4-mark combined question you reflect in the wrong line, then enlarge your own image correctly. What is still available?
options: The marks for the second stage
Nothing, because the first stage was wrong
All four marks
noteBlocks.answer: The marks for the second stage
noteBlocks.explain: CCEA marks positively: the enlargement is judged against the image you actually drew. The examiners recorded exactly this in Summer 2025. It is why a committed attempt beats a blank grid every time.

noteBlocks.md: **Order changes the answer.** Below, triangle T is reflected in $y = x$ and then rotated a quarter turn anticlockwise about the origin, giving U. Do the same two transformations the other way round and you get V instead. They are not the same triangle, so read the sentence carefully and start where it tells you to.

options: V
U
Both, since the order makes no difference
noteBlocks.explain: V is the rotate-first route. U comes from reflecting first. Reading the sentence from left to right and starting where it starts is the whole skill here.

noteBlocks.text: One transformation that does the work of two

noteBlocks.md:
Two transformations in a row always add up to a single one, and CCEA likes asking for it. Two cases are worth knowing by heart.

**Two reflections in perpendicular mirrors give a rotation of $180^\circ$ about the point where the mirrors cross.** $y = x$ and $y = -x$ are perpendicular and cross at the origin, so reflecting in one and then the other is a half turn about $(0, 0)$. A half turn needs no direction: clockwise and anticlockwise land in the same place.

A dashed segment from (2, 7) through the origin to (-2, -7) shows the half turn.

noteBlocks.prompt: A shape is reflected in the $x$-axis and then in the $y$-axis. The single transformation is
options: a rotation of $180^\circ$ about the origin
a reflection in the line $y = x$
a translation
noteBlocks.answer: a rotation of $180^\circ$ about the origin
noteBlocks.explain: The two axes are perpendicular and cross at the origin, so the pair is a half turn about $(0, 0)$. Two reflections never leave you with another reflection.

noteBlocks.md: **Two reflections in parallel mirrors give a translation**, perpendicular to the mirrors, of **twice** the gap between them. Below, the mirrors $x = -5$ and $x = -1$ are 4 apart, so P ends up 8 to the right — not 4. The doubling is the part that gets forgotten.

noteBlocks.prompt: A shape is reflected in $x = 2$ and then in $x = 7$. It ends up translated how many units to the right?
noteBlocks.explain: The mirrors are 5 apart and the translation is twice the gap: $2 \times 5 = 10$ to the right. Reflecting in the far mirror first would give 10 to the left instead.

noteBlocks.text: Describing: every detail, or no mark

noteBlocks.md: *Describe fully the single transformation…* is a 2- or 3-mark instruction with a checklist behind it, and the marks are handed out one per item on the list. Give the name and nothing else and you have one of three.

noteBlocks.prompt: You have drawn the middle image and you are running out of time. What do you do with it?
options: Leave it on the grid and label it
Rub it out so only the final answer is showing
Cross it out neatly
noteBlocks.answer: Leave it on the grid and label it
noteBlocks.explain: It is worth marks in its own right — typically two of the four. The reports record candidates erasing a correct first image and losing those marks. Crossed-out work is still marked, but there is no reason to cross out something correct.

noteBlocks.title: The four checklists
noteBlocks.md:
**Reflection** — the word *reflection*, and the **equation of the mirror line** ($y = x$, not "the diagonal"). [2 marks]
**Rotation** — the word *rotation*, the **angle**, the **direction** (unless it is $180^\circ$), and the **centre** as a coordinate pair. [3 marks]
**Translation** — the word *translation* and the **column vector**. [2 marks]
**Enlargement** — the word *enlargement*, the **scale factor** (with its sign), and the **centre**. [3 marks]
And one rule over all four: **the question says single, so write one transformation.** A description made of two transformations joined by "then" scores zero, however well it describes the picture.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these earns all three marks?
options: Rotation, $90^\circ$ clockwise, about $(2, -1)$
Turned $90^\circ$ about $(2, -1)$
Rotation of $90^\circ$ about the centre
Reflection in $y = x$ then a translation
noteBlocks.explain: Name, angle, direction, centre. "Turned" is not the word *rotation* and loses the naming mark; "about the centre" names no point; and the last one describes two transformations when the question asked for one.

noteBlocks.md: **Finding the centre of a rotation.** Join a vertex to its image and construct the perpendicular bisector of that join. Do it again for a second vertex. The centre is where the two bisectors cross — it is the only point that is the same distance from each vertex as it is from that vertex's image. On a grid you can usually spot the crossing point by eye once the two bisectors are drawn.

noteBlocks.md: **Finding the centre of an enlargement.** Join each vertex of the image to the matching vertex of the object and extend the lines. All of them meet at the centre. The scale factor is the image length divided by the object length, using a pair of matching sides — and if the image is the smaller shape, that fraction is less than 1, which is exactly what a fractional scale factor means.

noteBlocks.prompt: How should the translation in the figure above be written?
options: A translation by the column vector with 5 on top and $-7$ underneath
A translation to $(-2, -4)$
A translation of 5 and 7
noteBlocks.answer: A translation by the column vector with 5 on top and $-7$ underneath
noteBlocks.explain: The top number is the movement across and the bottom number is the movement up, so down is negative. A coordinate pair names a place, not a movement, and "5 and 7" says nothing about direction.

noteBlocks.title: Not on this specification
noteBlocks.md: Rotations are limited to $90^\circ$ either way and $180^\circ$, so you will never be asked for $30^\circ$ or $45^\circ$. Matrices are not used for transformations anywhere in this course. Negative scale factors belong to M8 and are not part of these two statements, and invariant points and glide reflections are not on the specification at all. What you do need is everything from M5 and M6 — reflections in the axes and in lines like $x = 3$, rotations about any point, translations by a column vector — because a combined question is built out of them.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these could be asked in an M7 or M8 combined-transformation question?
options: A rotation of $180^\circ$ about $(2, 1)$
A rotation of $45^\circ$ about the origin
A transformation given as a 2 by 2 matrix
noteBlocks.explain: The Teacher Guidance limits rotations to a quarter turn either way and a half turn, about any point. Angles like $45^\circ$ and matrix transformations are not on this specification, so you never have to prepare for them.

noteBlocks.md:
Swap the coordinates for $y = x$; swap and change signs for $y = -x$.
Do the transformations in the order given, and keep the middle image.
Describe with the full checklist: one transformation, every detail.

M7 and M8 both set this, usually among the last four questions, worth 2 to 4 marks. Doing two transformations earns a mark per correct image, so the middle one is never rubbed out. Describing earns nothing unless it is one transformation with every detail. Stuck: draw the mirror line first and reflect a single vertex, then count the squares back.

Draw the image of T after a reflection in $y = x$, and then an enlargement, scale factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$, about $(-5, -2)$.

Label the first image T' and the final image T".

steps.decision: The mirror goes on the grid before anything is reflected. It costs four seconds and it is the single thing that stops the image landing in the wrong place.
A reflection in $y = x$ swaps each pair of coordinates. I take the vertices one at a time and write each image down before I draw it, so there is a record even if the drawing goes wrong.

options: Because reflecting in $y = x$ exchanges the across and up parts of each point
Because both coordinates change sign
Because the shape moves 2 to the right
whyMenu.explain: The line $y = x$ is where the two coordinates are equal, so reflecting in it swaps their roles. Changing both signs would be a reflection in $y = -x$.

steps.working: Draw T' at $(1, 2)$, $(7, 2)$, $(1, 6)$ and label it. Leave it there.
steps.decision: This first image is worth marks on its own. Rubbing it out once the second stage is drawn is the presentation slip the reports keep recording.

steps.working: From $(-5, -2)$: to $(1, 2)$ is 6 across, 4 up. Half is 3 across, 2 up $\to (-2, 0)$.
steps.decision: An enlargement measures from the centre, not from the origin and not from the shape. I count the steps across and up separately, halve each one, and that is the image vertex.

steps.working: $(7, 2)$: 12 across, 4 up $\to$ 6 across, 2 up $\to (1, 0)$. $(1, 6)$: 6 across, 8 up $\to$ 3 across, 4 up $\to (-2, 2)$.
steps.decision: The same counting for the other two vertices. The scale factor is a half, so the image is half as far from the centre in every direction — and half the size.
Both images are on the grid and both are labelled, so the marker can follow the order without guessing which triangle came first.

workedExamples.stem:
Triangle C has vertices $(2, 5)$, $(2, 7)$ and $(5, 5)$.

(a) Reflect C in the line $y = x$ and label the image C'.
(b) Reflect C' in the line $y = -x$ and label the image C".
(c) Describe fully the single transformation that maps C onto C".

steps.decision: Swap each pair for the reflection in $y = x$. The vertex $(5, 5)$ sits on the mirror, so it does not move — a useful check that the mirror is drawn where I think it is.
Now the second mirror acts on C', not on C. For $y = -x$ I swap and then change both signs.
Every coordinate has had its sign changed and nothing else. That is the fingerprint of a half turn about the origin.

options: Because the two mirrors are perpendicular, so the pair is a rotation about the point where they cross
Because two reflections always give another reflection
Because the shape has moved, so it must be a translation
whyMenu.explain: $y = x$ and $y = -x$ meet at right angles at the origin. Two reflections in perpendicular mirrors always give a rotation of $180^\circ$ about their crossing point.

steps.decision: Three items: the name, the angle, the centre. A half turn needs no direction, because clockwise and anticlockwise finish in the same place. One transformation, not two.

steps.working: P is 8 wide and 4 tall; Q is 4 wide and 2 tall. Same angles, different size.
steps.decision: Size has changed, so it is an enlargement. Reflections, rotations and translations all leave lengths alone, which rules them out in one glance.
Image over object, using a matching pair of sides. Q is the image, so the fraction is less than 1. Writing 2 would describe the enlargement the other way round.

steps.working: Join $(-7, -3)$ to $(-4, 1)$ and extend; join $(1, -3)$ to $(0, 1)$ and extend.
steps.decision: The centre is where the vertex joins meet. Two of them are enough to fix the point; a third is a free check.

steps.working: The lines meet at $(-1, 5)$. Check: $(-1, 5)$ to $(-7, -3)$ is $(-6, -8)$; half of that is $(-3, -4)$, landing on $(-4, 1)$.
steps.decision: I verify the centre by walking half way along one ray. If it lands on the image vertex, the centre and the scale factor agree with each other.
Three items on one line. Leaving the centre out is what the Summer 2025 report singled out, and it is a third of the marks.

steps.working: G and H are the same size, and G has been turned: its long side runs across, H's runs down.
steps.decision: Same size rules out an enlargement. The shape is not simply slid along, so it is not a translation. A reflection would give a mirror image; this one has been turned, so it is a rotation.

steps.working: The long side of G points right; on H it points down. Right turned to down is a quarter turn clockwise.
steps.decision: I read the angle and the direction off one side rather than off the whole shape, because one side has an unambiguous direction.

options: Because a side pointing right becomes a side pointing down after a quarter turn clockwise
Because the shape has moved to the right
Because the shape is below the x-axis
whyMenu.explain: Track one side, not the whole triangle. Right becoming down is $90^\circ$ clockwise; right becoming up would be $90^\circ$ anticlockwise.

steps.working: Join $(3, 1)$ to $(5, -3)$ and bisect it at right angles; join $(7, 1)$ to $(5, -7)$ and do the same.
steps.decision: The centre is the same distance from a vertex as from its image, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector of the join. Two bisectors pin it down.
I test it: a quarter turn clockwise about $(2, -2)$ sends $(3, 1)$ to $(5, -3)$, which is where H's vertex is.
Name, angle, direction, centre. Writing $270^\circ$ anticlockwise instead would also be accepted, because it is the same turn; writing "turn" instead of "rotation" would not.

items.stem: The point $(4, 7)$ is reflected in $y = x$. Where is its image?
items.skill: Reflect a point in the line y = x

options.feedback: Reflecting in $y = x$ swaps the pair, so $(4, 7)$ becomes $(7, 4)$. On the grid, check that the join between them crosses the mirror at a right angle.
That is the reflection in the $y$-axis. The examiners see this one every series: draw $y = x$ on the grid first and the slip disappears.
That is the reflection in the $x$-axis. Reflecting in $y = x$ leaves both signs alone and swaps the numbers instead.
You swapped and then changed both signs, which is the rule for $y = -x$. For $y = x$ the swap is the whole of it.

items.stem: The point $(4, 7)$ is reflected in $y = -x$. Where is its image?
items.skill: Reflect a point in the line y = -x

options.feedback: Swap to $(7, 4)$, then change both signs to $(-7, -4)$. Two moves, in that order.
You did the swap but stopped there, which is the $y = x$ answer. The second mirror also reverses both directions.
You changed both signs without swapping. That is a rotation of $180^\circ$ about the origin, not a reflection.
That is the reflection in the $y$-axis. The mirror here is the falling diagonal, so both coordinates are involved.
Each $y$-coordinate is the negative of its $x$-coordinate, so it is the diagonal that falls from left to right.

options.text: $y = x$
options.feedback: On $y = x$ the two coordinates are equal, so it would pass through $(2, 2)$ and $(-5, -5)$. This line does the opposite.

options.text: the $x$-axis
options.feedback: The $x$-axis is $y = 0$ and passes through $(2, 0)$, not $(2, -2)$.

options.text: $x = -y$ only, which is a different line from $y = -x$
options.feedback: $x = -y$ and $y = -x$ are two ways of writing the same line; rearranging one gives the other.

items.stem: A shape is reflected in $y = x$, and that image is then reflected in $y = -x$. What single transformation has the same effect?
items.skill: Combine two reflections in perpendicular mirrors

options.text: A rotation of $180^\circ$ about the origin
options.feedback: The two mirrors are perpendicular and cross at the origin, so the pair is a half turn about $(0, 0)$. No direction is needed for $180^\circ$.

options.text: A reflection in the $y$-axis
options.feedback: Two reflections never leave you with another reflection: each one reverses the sense of the shape, so two put it back.

options.text: A rotation of $90^\circ$ clockwise about the origin
options.feedback: The angle of the rotation is twice the angle between the mirrors. These two are $90^\circ$ apart, so the turn is $180^\circ$.

options.text: A translation
options.feedback: A translation comes from two reflections in **parallel** mirrors. These two cross, so the result is a rotation about the crossing point.

items.stem: Which answer would earn all three marks for describing a rotation?
items.skill: Know what a full description of a rotation contains

options.text: Rotation, $90^\circ$ anticlockwise, about $(3, -2)$
options.feedback: Name, angle, direction, centre. That is the complete checklist, and $270^\circ$ clockwise would be accepted for the middle two.

options.text: Turned $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about $(3, -2)$
options.feedback: Everything else is right, but "turned" is not the word *rotation* and the naming mark goes. The reports name this one directly.

options.text: Rotation of $90^\circ$ about the centre of the grid
options.feedback: The angle is there but the direction is missing and the centre is not a coordinate pair. Two of the three items are unmarked.

options.text: Rotation $90^\circ$ anticlockwise, then a translation 2 to the right
options.feedback: The question asks for a *single* transformation. A description made of two scores zero however well it fits the picture.

items.stem: A shape is reflected in the line $x = 1$, and that image is reflected in the line $x = 5$. What single transformation has the same effect?
items.skill: Combine two reflections in parallel mirrors

options.text: A translation of 8 to the right
options.feedback: The mirrors are 4 apart and the translation is twice the gap. The doubling is the part most often missed.

options.text: A translation of 4 to the right
options.feedback: 4 is the gap between the mirrors. Reflecting twice carries the shape across the gap and out the same distance again, so it moves 8.

options.text: A reflection in $x = 3$
options.feedback: $x = 3$ is halfway between the mirrors, but two reflections cannot give a reflection: the shape comes back the right way round.

options.text: A rotation of $180^\circ$ about $(3, 0)$
options.feedback: A rotation comes from two mirrors that cross. These two are parallel, so nothing turns.

items.stem: The point $(8, 6)$ is enlarged by scale factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ with centre $(2, 2)$. Where is its image?
items.skill: Enlarge a point by a fractional scale factor about a given centre

options.feedback: From $(2, 2)$ to $(8, 6)$ is 6 across and 4 up. Half of that is 3 across and 2 up, landing on $(5, 4)$.
You halved the coordinates themselves, which is what happens only when the centre is the origin. Count from $(2, 2)$ instead.
That is the centre. The image sits part of the way along the ray, not on top of the centre — a slip the Summer 2025 report records.
That is scale factor 2: you doubled the distances instead of halving them. A scale factor below 1 brings the image closer to the centre.

items.stem: *Reflect the shape in $y = x$, followed by a translation 3 units down.* What does the translation act on?
items.skill: Apply two transformations in the stated order

options.text: The image produced by the reflection
options.feedback: Each transformation acts on whatever the one before it produced, which is why the middle image has to exist before you start the second step.

options.text: The original shape, then the two images are compared
options.feedback: That gives two separate images of the original, not a combination. The word *followed by* chains them together.

options.text: Either, because the final image is the same both ways
options.feedback: Swapping the order generally moves the final image somewhere else. Only in special cases do two transformations commute.

options.text: The original shape, and the reflection is then applied to that
options.feedback: That is the reverse order. Read left to right and start with the transformation named first.

context.setting: A single point on a coordinate grid, no context

parts.stem:
The point $A$ has coordinates $(6, -2)$.

Write down the coordinates of the image of $A$ after a reflection in $y = x$.
hints: Reflecting in $y = x$ swaps the two coordinates.
The signs are not touched — swap the pair exactly as it stands.
parts.workedSolution: Reflection in $y = x$ swaps the coordinates, so $(6, -2) \to (-2, 6)$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the reflection in the $y$-axis. Draw $y = x$ on the grid and the two answers stop looking alike.
You swapped and then changed both signs, which is the rule for $y = -x$. For $y = x$ the swap is the whole of it.

questions.solutionProgram: reflect (6, -2) in y = x: swap the pair -> (-2, 6)

parts.stem: Describe fully the single transformation that takes triangle $E$ to triangle $F$.
hints: The sense of the triangle is reversed, so it is a reflection.
Take one vertex and its image: what happened to the numbers and to the signs?
Give the mirror as an equation.
parts.workedSolution: $(2, 4) \to (-4, -2)$: the coordinates are swapped and both signs are changed, which is the rule for the mirror $y = -x$.

commonErrors.feedback: $y = x$ would leave the triangle in the first quadrant. Both signs have changed as well, so the mirror is the falling diagonal.
A rotation of $180^\circ$ would keep the triangle the same way round; here the sense is reversed, which only a reflection does.

questions.solutionProgram: each vertex of F is the vertex of E swapped and negated, so the mirror is y = -x

context.setting: A single point on a coordinate grid, no context

parts.stem:
The point $B$ has coordinates $(-3, 5)$.

$B$ is reflected in $y = x$, and that image is then reflected in $y = -x$.

Write down the coordinates of the final image.
hints: After the first reflection the point is at $(5, -3)$.
Now apply the second rule to that point, not to $B$.
Check: two perpendicular mirrors make a half turn about the origin.
parts.workedSolution: $(-3, 5) \to (5, -3)$ in $y = x$, then $(5, -3) \to (3, -5)$ in $y = -x$. Both signs of $B$ have simply been changed, which is the half turn about the origin that two perpendicular mirrors always produce.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the image after the first reflection only. It is worth writing down, but the second mirror still has to act on it.

questions.solutionProgram: reflect (-3, 5) in y = x -> (5, -3); reflect that in y = -x -> (3, -5); a half turn about the origin gives the same point

context.setting: A triangle on a coordinate grid, no context

figures.alt: A coordinate grid from -8 to 8 with the dashed line y = x. Triangle G has vertices at (1, 2), (1, 6) and (4, 2).

parts.stem:
Triangle $G$ has vertices $(1, 2)$, $(1, 6)$ and $(4, 2)$.

Draw $G'$, the image of $G$ after a reflection in $y = x$.

scheme.for: reflection in y = x attempted, at least two vertices swapped

hints: Draw the line $y = x$ on the grid first.
Swap each pair of coordinates in turn.
Leave $G'$ drawn and labelled — it carries two of this question's four marks on its own.
parts.workedSolution: Reflecting in $y = x$ swaps each pair: (1, 2), (1, 6), (4, 2) becomes (2, 1), (6, 1), (2, 4).

pattern.test: image drawn at (-1, 2), (-1, 6), (-4, 2), the reflection in the y-axis

commonErrors.feedback: A reflection in the $y$-axis puts $G'$ at (-1, 2), (-1, 6), (-4, 2). The mirror here is the rising diagonal, so the coordinates swap and the signs stay as they are.

parts.stem:
Draw $G''$, the image of $G'$ after a translation 6 units left and 4 units down.

(So $G''$ is the image of $G$ after a reflection in $y = x$, followed by that translation.)

scheme.for: the translation applied to the candidate's own G'

hints: Work from $G'$, not from $G$.
6 left and 4 down means subtract 6 from each $x$ and 4 from each $y$.
The shape does not turn or change size, so check that $G''$ looks exactly like $G'$.

pattern.test: image drawn at (-5, -2), (-5, 2), (-2, -2), the translation applied to G instead of to G'

commonErrors.feedback: Translating the original triangle gives (-5, -2), (-5, 2), (-2, -2). The second transformation acts on the image the first one made, so start from $G'$.

pattern.test: image drawn at (-2, -5), (2, -5), (-2, -2), the two components of the vector swapped

commonErrors.feedback: That is 4 left and 6 down, with the two numbers the wrong way round. The first number is the movement across and the second is the movement up or down.

questions.solutionProgram: reflect in y = x, then translate the image 6 left and 4 down

context.setting: A triangle and its final image on a coordinate grid, no context

parts.stem:
Triangle $H$ is reflected in $y = x$. That image is then reflected in $y = -x$, giving triangle $J$.

Describe fully the single transformation that maps $H$ onto $J$.
hints: The two mirrors are perpendicular. What do two perpendicular mirrors always give?
Where do $y = x$ and $y = -x$ cross?
A half turn needs no direction.
parts.workedSolution: Reflecting (3, 1), (6, 1), (6, 3) in $y = x$ gives (1, 3), (1, 6), (3, 6), and reflecting that in $y = -x$ gives (-3, -1), (-6, -1), (-6, -3). Every coordinate has had its sign changed, which is a rotation of $180^\circ$ about the origin — the point where the two perpendicular mirrors cross.

commonErrors.feedback: Describing the two reflections again scores nothing: the question asks what single transformation does the same job.
Two reflections put the sense of the shape back the right way round, so the result can never be another reflection.
The word alone is one of three marks. The angle and the centre are the other two, and both are short to write.

questions.solutionProgram: reflect H in y = x, then that image in y = -x; the pair is a rotation of 180 degrees about the origin

context.setting: Two congruent triangles on a coordinate grid, no context

parts.stem: Describe fully the single transformation that takes triangle $K$ to triangle $L$.
hints: Same size, turned round: that is a rotation.
Track one side: the long side of $K$ points up, and on $L$ it points to the right.
Join a vertex to its image and construct the perpendicular bisector; do it twice and the centre is where they cross.
parts.workedSolution: Joining $(-5, 1)$ to $(1, 3)$ and $(-5, 4)$ to $(4, 3)$ and bisecting both at right angles gives a crossing point at $(-1, -1)$. A quarter turn clockwise about that point maps (-5, 1), (-5, 4), (-3, 1) onto (1, 3), (4, 3), (1, 1).

commonErrors.feedback: The origin is the default guess, not the answer. Construct the centre from two perpendicular bisectors and it comes out at $(-1, -1)$.
Check the direction on one side: the long side of $K$ points upwards and ends up pointing right, which is clockwise. $270^\circ$ anticlockwise says the same thing.
"Turn" is not the word the scheme wants. Write *rotation* and the naming mark is safe.

questions.solutionProgram: perpendicular bisectors of two vertex joins meet at (-1, -1); a quarter turn clockwise about it maps K onto L

context.setting: Two similar triangles on a coordinate grid, no context

parts.stem: Describe fully the single transformation that takes triangle $M$ to triangle $N$.
hints: The size has changed and the angles have not, so it is an enlargement.
Scale factor is image length over object length.
Join each vertex of $N$ to the matching vertex of $M$ and extend the lines until they meet.
parts.workedSolution: The vertical side of $M$ is 6 and the vertical side of $N$ is 2, so the scale factor is $\tfrac{2}{6} = \tfrac{1}{3}$. Joining $(-6, -6)$ to $(0, 0)$ and $(-6, 0)$ to $(0, 2)$ and extending, the lines meet at $(3, 3)$.

commonErrors.feedback: The centre is a third of this question. It is the one part you can construct rather than estimate: join corresponding vertices and extend.
3 describes the enlargement from $N$ to $M$. Going the way the question asks, the image is the smaller triangle, so the scale factor is below 1.

questions.solutionProgram: scale factor = 2/6 = 1/3; the vertex joins meet at (3, 3)

parts.stem:
Triangle $P$ is reflected in the line $x = -3$. That image is then reflected in the line $x = 1$, giving triangle $R$.

Describe fully the single transformation that maps $P$ onto $R$.
hints: Two parallel mirrors cannot turn or flip the shape, so what is left?
How far apart are the mirrors?
The shape moves twice that distance.
parts.workedSolution: Reflecting (-7, 2), (-4, 2), (-7, 5) in $x = -3$ gives (1, 2), (-2, 2), (1, 5), and reflecting that in $x = 1$ gives (1, 2), (4, 2), (1, 5). Every vertex has moved 8 to the right — twice the 4-unit gap between the mirrors — so it is a translation by the column vector with 8 on top and 0 underneath.

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is the gap between the mirrors. The shape crosses that gap and comes out the same distance again on the far side, so it travels 8.
The top number of a column vector is the movement across and the bottom one is the movement up. Here nothing moves vertically.

questions.solutionProgram: two parallel mirrors 4 apart give a translation of 2 x 4 = 8 in the x direction

context.setting: A single vertex of a shape on a coordinate grid, no context

parts.stem:
A shape is reflected in $y = x$, and the image is then rotated $90^\circ$ clockwise about the origin.

One vertex of the shape is at $V(2, 5)$. Write down the coordinates of the image of $V$.
hints: Do the reflection first and write the point down.
A quarter turn clockwise about the origin sends $(x, y)$ to $(y, -x)$.
Try it on a point you can picture, such as $(1, 0)$, if you are unsure of the direction.
parts.workedSolution: The reflection gives $(2, 5) \to (5, 2)$. A quarter turn clockwise about the origin then sends $(5, 2)$ to $(2, -5)$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the reflection of V in y = -x, which swaps the coordinates and changes both signs. Reflection in y = x only swaps them: V(2, 5) goes to (5, 2). Then the clockwise quarter turn sends (5, 2) to (2, -5).

That is the image if the quarter turn went the other way, and also what you get by rotating first and reflecting afterwards. Clockwise sends $(x, y)$ to $(y, -x)$; anticlockwise sends it to $(-y, x)$. The order in the sentence is the order on the page: reflect first, then rotate.

questions.solutionProgram: reflect (2, 5) in y = x -> (5, 2); rotate 90 degrees clockwise about the origin -> (2, -5)

figures.alt: A coordinate grid from -8 to 8 with the dashed line y = -x. Triangle W has vertices at (2, 2), (6, 2) and (2, 6). A ringed cross marks the centre of enlargement at (2, 2).

parts.stem:
Triangle $W$ has vertices $(2, 2)$, $(6, 2)$ and $(2, 6)$.

Draw $W'$, the image of $W$ after a reflection in $y = -x$.

scheme.for: reflection in y = -x attempted, at least two vertices swapped and negated

hints: Swap each pair of coordinates, then change both signs.
The mirror falls from the top left to the bottom right; draw it first.
Leave $W'$ drawn and labelled — it carries two of this question's four marks.
parts.workedSolution: Reflecting in $y = -x$ swaps each pair and changes both signs: (2, 2), (6, 2), (2, 6) becomes (-2, -2), (-2, -6), (-6, -2).

pattern.test: image drawn at (-2, 2), (-6, 2), (-2, 6), the reflection in the y-axis

commonErrors.feedback: The $y$-axis only changes the sign of each $x$-coordinate, which puts $W'$ at (-2, 2), (-6, 2), (-2, 6). The falling diagonal swaps the pair as well.

parts.stem:
Draw $W''$, the image of $W'$ after an enlargement, scale factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$, about $(2, 2)$.

(So $W''$ is the image of $W$ after a reflection in $y = -x$, followed by that enlargement.)

scheme.for: rays from (2, 2) to the candidate's own W', distances halved

hints: Count across and up from $(2, 2)$ to each vertex of $W'$.
Halve both counts and mark the point you reach.
The image is half the size of $W'$, so check its side lengths when you have drawn it.
parts.workedSolution: From the centre $(2, 2)$, vertex $(-2, -2)$ is 4 left and 4 down; half of that is 2 left and 2 down, giving $(0, 0)$. The same counting gives $(0, -2)$ and $(-2, 0)$.

pattern.test: image drawn at (-1, -1), (-1, -3), (-3, -1), the coordinates halved from the origin instead of from the given centre

commonErrors.feedback: Halving the coordinates themselves gives (-1, -1), (-1, -3), (-3, -1), which is the enlargement about the origin. The centre is the point you measure from, and here it is $(2, 2)$.

pattern.test: image drawn at (2, 2), (4, 2), (2, 4), the enlargement applied to W instead of to W'

commonErrors.feedback: Enlarging the original triangle gives (2, 2), (4, 2), (2, 4). The enlargement acts on the reflected image, so start from $W'$.

questions.solutionProgram: reflect in y = -x, then enlarge the image by 1/2 about (2, 2)

emphasis: reflection in y = x then fractional enlargement

parts.stem: Draw $T'$, the image of triangle $T$ after a reflection in $y = x$.
hints: Draw $y = x$ before you reflect anything.
Write the three swapped vertices down before you draw them.
Leave $T'$ on the grid: it is worth two marks whatever happens next.
parts.workedSolution: Reflecting in $y = x$ swaps each pair, so (1, 2), (7, 2), (1, 6) becomes (2, 1), (2, 7), (6, 1).

pattern.test: image drawn at (-1, 2), (-7, 2), (-1, 6), the reflection in the y-axis

commonErrors.feedback: The $y$-axis puts $T'$ at (-1, 2), (-7, 2), (-1, 6). Even so, the next part is still worth having: enlarge whatever you drew, carefully, and those marks are there.

parts.stem:
Draw $F$, the image of $T'$ after an enlargement, scale factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$, about $(-6, -1)$.

(So $F$ is the image of $T$ after a reflection in $y = x$, followed by that enlargement.)

scheme.for: enlargement of the candidate's own T' from (-6, -1), distances halved

hints: From $(-6, -1)$, count across and up to each vertex of $T'$.
Halve both counts and mark the point you land on.
Check the finished triangle is half the size of $T'$.
parts.workedSolution: From $(-6, -1)$, vertex $(2, 1)$ is 8 across and 2 up; halving gives 4 across and 1 up, which is $(-2, 0)$. The other two vertices give $(-2, 3)$ and $(0, 0)$, so $F$ is the triangle (-2, 0), (-2, 3), (0, 0).

pattern.test: image drawn at (-2, 1), (-2, 4), (0, 1), the sign of the centre's y-coordinate misread so the counting started from the wrong point

commonErrors.feedback: Reading the centre as $(-6, 1)$ puts the image at (-2, 1), (-2, 4), (0, 1). Mark the centre on the grid before you count, and check its sign against the question.

questions.solutionProgram: reflect T in y = x, then enlarge the image by 1/2 about (-6, -1)

parts.stem: Describe fully the single transformation that takes shape $A$ to shape $B$.
hints: Compare a matching pair of sides to get the scale factor.
Join each vertex of $B$ to the matching vertex of $A$.
Extend those joins until they cross; that crossing point is the centre.
parts.workedSolution: The vertical side of $A$ is 6 and of $B$ is 2, so the scale factor is $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Joining $(-8, -1)$ to $(0, -3)$ and $(-8, 5)$ to $(0, -1)$ and extending, the lines meet at $(4, -4)$. Check: $(4, -4)$ to $(-2, -1)$ is 6 left and 3 up, and a third of that is 2 left and 1 up, landing on $(2, -3)$.

parts.stem:
Triangle $P$ has vertices $(1, 3)$, $(1, 6)$ and $(3, 3)$.

Reflect $P$ in the line $y = x$. Label the image $P'$.

scheme.examinerNote: Award 1 mark for two vertices in the correct position.

hints: Swap the coordinates of each vertex.
The vertex $(3, 3)$ is on the mirror, so it stays where it is.
parts.workedSolution: Swapping each pair: (1, 3), (1, 6), (3, 3) becomes (3, 1), (6, 1), (3, 3). The vertex $(3, 3)$ lies on the mirror and does not move.

pattern.test: image drawn at (-1, 3), (-1, 6), (-3, 3), the reflection in the y-axis

commonErrors.feedback: The $y$-axis sends the triangle to (-1, 3), (-1, 6), (-3, 3); $y = x$ sends it down and right instead. Drawing the mirror first separates the two.

parts.stem: Reflect $P'$ in the $x$-axis. Label the image $P''$.

scheme.for: correct reflection of the candidate's own P', vertices (3, -1), (6, -1), (3, -3)
scheme.examinerNote: Follow through from part (a); award 1 mark for two vertices in the correct position.

hints: A reflection in the $x$-axis changes the sign of each $y$-coordinate.
Work from $P'$, not from $P$.
parts.workedSolution: Changing the sign of each $y$-coordinate of (3, 1), (6, 1), (3, 3) gives (3, -1), (6, -1), (3, -3).

pattern.test: image drawn at (1, -3), (1, -6), (3, -3), the x-axis reflection applied to P instead of to P'

commonErrors.feedback: Reflecting the original triangle in the $x$-axis gives (1, -3), (1, -6), (3, -3). The second mirror acts on the image the first one made, so start from $P'$.

parts.stem: Describe fully the single transformation that maps $P$ onto $P''$.
hints: The two mirrors cross at the origin, so the single transformation is a rotation about it.
Follow one vertex from $P$ to $P''$ to read off the direction.
The angle is twice the angle between the mirrors.
parts.workedSolution: $(1, 3)$ ends up at $(3, -1)$ and $(1, 6)$ at $(6, -1)$: each point $(x, y)$ has become $(y, -x)$, which is a quarter turn clockwise about the origin. The mirrors $y = x$ and the $x$-axis meet at $45^\circ$, and the rotation is twice that.

commonErrors.feedback: Repeating the two reflections describes the picture but not what the question asked. One rotation does the same job.
Follow one vertex: $(1, 6)$ finishes at $(6, -1)$, which is a quarter turn clockwise. Anticlockwise would send it to $(-6, 1)$.

questions.solutionProgram: reflect P in y = x, reflect that in the x-axis; the pair is a quarter turn clockwise about the origin

emphasis: a reflection is its own inverse

figures.alt: A coordinate grid from -8 to 8 with the dashed line y = -x. Triangle T has vertices at (2, 1), (6, 1), (6, 3).

parts.stem:
Triangle $T$ has vertices $(2, 1)$, $(6, 1)$ and $(6, 3)$.

Reflect $T$ in the line $y = -x$. Label the image $U$.

scheme.examinerNote: Award 1 mark for two vertices in the correct position.

hints: Swap each pair of coordinates, then change both signs.
Every vertex should end up the same distance from the mirror as it started.
parts.workedSolution: (2, 1), (6, 1), (6, 3) becomes (-1, -2), (-1, -6), (-3, -6): each pair is swapped and then both signs are changed.

pattern.test: image drawn at (1, 2), (1, 6), (3, 6), the coordinates swapped without the sign change

commonErrors.feedback: Swapping alone is the rule for $y = x$ and puts the image at (1, 2), (1, 6), (3, 6). This mirror falls from left to right, so both signs change as well.

parts.stem: Describe fully the single transformation that maps $U$ back onto $T$.
hints: Reflect $U$ in the same mirror and see where it lands.
What happens if you swap and negate a pair of coordinates twice?
parts.workedSolution: Reflecting (-1, -2), (-1, -6), (-3, -6) in $y = -x$ swaps and negates each pair again, which returns (2, 1), (6, 1), (6, 3). A reflection is its own inverse, so the same line does the journey back.

commonErrors.feedback: One reflection takes $U$ straight back to $T$. Adding a second transformation turns a complete answer into a combination, which earns nothing.
A rotation would keep the triangle the same way round. Reflecting reverses its sense, and reflecting again puts it back.

questions.solutionProgram: reflect T in y = -x to get U; reflecting U in the same line returns T

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked to draw the image of a triangle with vertices $(3, 1)$, $(8, 1)$ and $(3, 4)$ after a reflection in $y = x$. Her working:
studentWorking: The mirror is a sloping line through the middle of the grid.
So the image is the triangle (-3, 1), (-8, 1), (-3, 4).
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 changes the sign of the first coordinate, which is a reflection in the $y$-axis. A reflection in $y = x$ leaves the signs alone and swaps the two numbers instead. Line 1 is where it really went wrong: the mirror was never drawn, so there was nothing to check against.
correction: Draw y = x on the grid, through (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2) and so on.
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing is lost that four seconds would not have saved. Every series the reports name this slip: the shape reflected in an axis when a diagonal was asked for. Draw the mirror line first and it becomes very hard to make.

findTheMistake.stem: Ciara was asked: *Describe fully the single transformation that takes shape A to shape B.* Her answer:
studentWorking: A and B are the same size, so nothing has been enlarged.
Reflect A in the line y = x.
Then translate that image 4 units down.
So the transformation is a reflection in y = x followed by a translation 4 down.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 4 gives two transformations when the question asked for one. The description may be a perfectly accurate account of the picture, and it still scores zero, because *single transformation* is an instruction rather than a hint.
correction: Read the instruction again: one transformation, with all of its details.
Same size and turned round, not flipped: that is a rotation.
Construct the centre from the perpendicular bisectors of two vertex joins.
Write: rotation, then the angle, then the direction, then the centre.
findTheMistake.feedback: The mathematics behind lines 1 to 3 is sound, and that is worth knowing. The marks went on the last line. When a description needs the word "then", it is not the answer the question wants, so go back and find the one transformation that does the whole job.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoife was asked to describe fully the single transformation that maps a triangle with vertices $(-6, -6)$, $(-6, 0)$ and $(-3, -6)$ onto a triangle with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(0, 2)$ and $(1, 0)$. Her answer, for 3 marks:
studentWorking: The second triangle is smaller, so it is an enlargement.
The big triangle is 3 times the size of the small one.
So it is an enlargement with scale factor 3.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Two things happen on line 3. The scale factor is written the wrong way round: it is measured from the object to the image, so a shrinking enlargement has a scale factor below 1, here $\tfrac{1}{3}$. And the centre is missing altogether, which is a third of the marks on its own.
correction: Scale factor = image length ÷ object length = 2 ÷ 6 = 1/3.
Join (-6, -6) to (0, 0) and (-6, 0) to (0, 2), then extend both lines.
They meet at (3, 3), so that is the centre.
findTheMistake.feedback: The first mark is safe: the transformation was named. The Summer 2025 examiners reported exactly this pattern — the enlargement recognised, but only a minority giving both the centre and the scale factor. Both are short to write and the centre can be constructed rather than guessed.

prompts.prompt: A point $(a, b)$ is reflected in $y = x$. Where does it go?
prompts.answer: $(b, a)$ — the coordinates swap and the signs are untouched.

prompts.prompt: A point $(a, b)$ is reflected in $y = -x$. Where does it go?
prompts.answer: $(-b, -a)$ — swap the coordinates, then change both signs.

prompts.prompt: What is the first thing you do on the grid before reflecting in $y = x$ or $y = -x$?
prompts.answer: Draw the mirror line. $y = x$ rises through $(1, 1)$, $(2, 2)$; $y = -x$ falls through $(1, -1)$, $(-2, 2)$.

prompts.prompt: What must a full description of a rotation contain?
prompts.answer: The word rotation, the angle, the direction (unless it is $180^\circ$) and the centre as a coordinate pair.

prompts.prompt: What must a full description of an enlargement contain?
prompts.answer: The word enlargement, the scale factor with its sign, and the centre of enlargement.

prompts.prompt: What must a full description of a reflection, and of a translation, contain?
prompts.answer: A reflection needs the word reflection and the equation of the mirror line. A translation needs the word translation and the column vector.

prompts.prompt: Two reflections in perpendicular mirror lines are equivalent to which single transformation?
prompts.answer: A rotation of $180^\circ$ about the point where the two mirrors cross. No direction is needed for a half turn.

prompts.prompt: Two reflections in parallel mirror lines are equivalent to which single transformation?
prompts.answer: A translation perpendicular to the mirrors, of twice the distance between them.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the centre of a rotation from a shape and its image?
prompts.answer: Join two vertices to their images and construct the perpendicular bisector of each join. The centre is where the bisectors cross.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the centre of an enlargement from a shape and its image?
prompts.answer: Join each vertex of the image to the matching vertex of the object and extend the lines. They all meet at the centre.

prompts.prompt: In a combined transformation, why must the first image stay on the grid?
prompts.answer: It carries marks of its own — usually two of the four — and the second transformation is marked against it, so erasing it throws those marks away.

prompts.prompt: Two wording traps in *describe fully the single transformation*.
prompts.answer: Writing "turn" instead of *rotation*, and describing two transformations joined by "then" when one was asked for. The second scores zero however accurate it is.

findings.asked: Reflect a shape in y = x, then enlarge with scale factor 2 about a given centre.
findings.wentWrong: Some erased the reflection (worth two marks); some reflected in the y-axis; the scale factor or the centre (7, 2) was misused.
findings.rule: Leave every intermediate image on the grid.

findings.asked: A combination of two higher-grade transformations.
findings.wentWrong: Nearly half got full marks; weaker candidates found the reflection in y = x impossible and made no progress.
findings.rule: Draw the line y = x and reflect vertex by vertex.

findings.asked: Reflect in y = x, then enlarge with scale factor 0.5 about (-4, 0).
findings.wentWrong: Reflections in the axes or in y = -x were common; the scale factor was understood but the centre was not - some drew the image at the centre.
findings.rule: Rays from the centre through each vertex; halve the distances.

findings.wentWrong: Just over 40% correct; over 30% showed no understanding; others reflected in the wrong line but enlarged their image correctly for partial credit.
findings.rule: Even a wrong first stage can earn marks if the second is done properly to it.

findings.asked: Reflect a triangle in y = x.
findings.wentWrong: Most correct; some reflected in the y-axis or rotated by 180 degrees instead.
findings.rule: Draw y = x first - it is the mirror.

findings.wentWrong: Combinations of transformations score zero; 'turn' instead of rotate, wrong direction, or no centre lost marks.
findings.rule: One transformation, all its details: rotate, angle, direction, centre.

findings.wentWrong: 'Enlargement' was recognised; scale factor 3 or -3 was often wrong and few found the centre; adding a translation afterwards scored zero.
The transformation was recognised, but only a minority gave both the centre and the scale factor correctly.
findings.rule: Find the centre by joining corresponding vertices and extending.

insight.ruleToRemember: Draw the mirror line y = x on the grid and reflect point by point; for an enlargement draw rays from the centre; never erase an intermediate image; when describing, give ONE transformation with every detail.
insight.aStarSignal: A reflection in y = x followed by a fractional or negative enlargement about an off-origin centre, both images left visible.
